summary.text: The Little Ice Age was a period of regional cooling, strongest around the North Atlantic, rather than a true ice age covering the globe.
It is usually dated from the 16th to the 19th centuries, though some experts prefer a span from about 1300 to about 1850.
Proposed causes include low points in solar radiation, more volcanic activity, changes in ocean circulation and falls in human population.

facts.label: Southern Hemisphere start
facts.value: About two centuries later than in the north

items.prompt: Glaciers grew in Alaska, New Zealand and Patagonia during this era, but they peaked at quite different times. What does that suggest?

options.label: Largely separate regional changes, not one global freeze
The dating methods used must be wrong
The whole planet froze at once
Glaciers there were growing for unrelated non-climate reasons

items.explain: Different peak times point to largely independent regional climate changes rather than a globally synchronous increase in glaciation.

items.prompt: Alongside the Sun and volcanoes, scientists have suggested a surprising human factor in the cooling. What is it?

options.label: Smoke from early coal-burning workshops
Large falls in human population, such as from the Black Death
The spread of large cities across Europe
Cannon smoke from long wars

items.explain: Decreases in human population, such as from the Black Death and epidemics in the Americas, are among the proposed causes.

items.prompt: A massive volcano, Samalas, erupted in 1257, around when Atlantic pack ice began to grow. How might the two be linked?

options.label: The eruption's heat melted the pack ice back
They are unrelated; the timing is coincidence
Lava flows blocked warm ocean currents
A volcanic winter may have set off or deepened the cold

items.explain: The cold period was possibly triggered or enhanced by the Samalas eruption and the volcanic winter that followed.

items.prompt: If the Little Ice Age had been one global event, it should have started at the same time everywhere. When did it begin in the Southern Hemisphere?

options.label: About two centuries before the north
In the very same decade as the north
About two centuries after the north
Only after 1900

items.explain: In the Southern Hemisphere the beginning was delayed by about two centuries relative to the north.

items.prompt: Researchers radiocarbon-dated dead plants, roots still intact, found under ice caps on Baffin Island and Iceland. What do those dates mainly reveal?

options.label: When people first farmed those islands
When cold summers and ice growth set in
How warm the 20th century became
When the ice caps first formed long ago

items.explain: The dates showed cold summers and ice growth beginning abruptly between 1275 and 1300.

items.prompt: Ask several climate experts exactly when the Little Ice Age began. What are you likely to hear?

options.label: The same year, 1300, from everyone
That it began with the Black Death
That it began in 1650 everywhere
Different answers, since there is no consensus

items.explain: There is no consensus on its start, and definitions differ depending on the region and data used.

paragraphs.heading: Not a true ice age
paragraphs.text: The Little Ice Age was a period of regional cooling, strongest around the North Atlantic. Despite its name, it was not a true ice age covering the whole planet. It is usually placed between the 16th and 19th centuries, though some experts prefer about 1300 to about 1850. A major report by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change judged that its timing and reach point to largely separate regional changes, not one worldwide growth of ice. At most, the Northern Hemisphere cooled modestly.

paragraphs.heading: The coldest stretches
paragraphs.text: NASA's Earth Observatory picks out three especially cold intervals. They began about 1650, about 1770 and in 1850, with spells of slight warming between them. Climate reconstructions show relatively cool conditions in the 17th and early 19th centuries, while the 20th century comes out warmest. The Little Ice Age ended in the later 19th or the early 20th century.

paragraphs.heading: When it began
paragraphs.text: There is no agreement on when it started. In the 13th century, pack ice in the North Atlantic began pushing south, and glaciers in Greenland advanced. Researchers who radiocarbon-dated about 150 samples of dead plants found under ice caps on Baffin Island and Iceland concluded that cold summers and ice growth began suddenly between 1275 and 1300, then grew much stronger from 1430 to 1455. In the Northern Hemisphere the cooling began between 1200 and 1400 AD, while in the Southern Hemisphere it started about two centuries later.

paragraphs.heading: Possible causes
paragraphs.text: Many causes have been suggested: low points in the Sun's radiation, more volcanic activity, changes in ocean circulation, shifts in Earth's orbit and tilt, natural swings in climate, and falls in human population. The population losses proposed include the Black Death, the massacres of Genghis Khan and the epidemics in the Americas after European contact. One cold period may have been triggered or made worse by the huge eruption of the Samalas volcano in 1257 and the volcanic winter that followed.

paragraphs.heading: Glaciers around the world
paragraphs.text: Mountain glaciers grew in many regions outside Europe before the 20th century, including Alaska, New Zealand and Patagonia. But they reached their greatest size at quite different times, which again hints at separate regional changes rather than one global event. One reconstruction based on glacier lengths shows little change from 1600 to 1850, then a strong retreat.

paragraphs.heading: Winters in Central Europe
paragraphs.text: In 2021 the historian Christian Pfister and the climatologist Heinz Wanner rebuilt Central Europe's seasonal temperatures from documents. A winter-by-winter reconstruction from 1170 onward paints a different picture of this cold period. Cold winters were normal in the 14th century except from 1340 to 1377, and the 15th century was cold nearly throughout apart from the 1470s. Especially harsh winters came from 1565 to 1573 and again from 1587 to 1595. Cold winter spells grew longer and stronger from the 14th century on, peaking in the 15th, 17th and 19th centuries.
